title: Lesson 1: Common Causes of Workplace Conflict
summary: Many conflicts start as small operational problems. Recognise the real cause, communicate early, and do not let assumptions or accusations make it personal.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Understanding workplace disagreements, identifying causes of conflict, emotional awareness, prevention and teamwork

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine two therapists working at Zura Spa.

One therapist finishes her massage session and leaves the treatment room without replenishing the towels and massage oil. The second therapist enters the room shortly before her next appointment and discovers that the room is not ready.
Feeling frustrated, she says: "Why do you always leave your work for other people? I'm tired of cleaning up after you!"
The first therapist responds: "Excuse me? I'm not your servant. You also leave things undone sometimes!"
The conversation becomes heated. Other employees begin listening. One colleague supports the first therapist, while another supports the second.
Before long, a simple disagreement about room preparation has become a conflict involving several employees.

The original problem was that the treatment room was not properly prepared. However, the situation became more complicated because of several additional factors: an incomplete responsibility, frustration, accusatory language, defensive reactions, references to previous mistakes, and other employees taking sides.
The original issue could have been resolved through clear communication and accountability. Instead, the employees allowed their emotions and reactions to make the situation worse.
This is how many workplace conflicts begin: a small operational problem develops into a personal disagreement because it is not handled appropriately.
At Zura Spa, employees must learn to recognise the common causes of conflict so they can prevent unnecessary disagreements, address problems early and maintain healthy professional relationships.

sections.title: 2. What is workplace conflict?
paragraphs: Workplace conflict is a disagreement, tension or dispute between employees or groups arising from differences in opinions, expectations, responsibilities, communication, behaviour or interests.
Conflict may involve two colleagues, an employee and a supervisor, several members of a team, different work responsibilities, or disagreements about procedures or expectations.
Conflict does not always involve shouting or insults. Sometimes it appears through silence, avoidance, resentment, refusal to cooperate or repeated misunderstandings.
These situations can create workplace conflict when they are not managed constructively.
list: A receptionist and therapist disagree about an appointment change.
Two therapists argue about room preparation.
An employee feels unfairly treated by a supervisor.
A colleague becomes upset because another employee repeatedly arrives late.
Staff members disagree about the distribution of shared responsibilities.

sections.title: 3. Understanding the difference between disagreement and conflict
paragraphs: A disagreement occurs when people have different opinions, interpretations or preferences.
Conflict develops when those differences create tension, interfere with relationships or affect cooperation.
Having different opinions is normal. Allowing those differences to become insults, resentment or hostility is what creates unnecessary conflict.
Not every disagreement must become a conflict.

sections.title: Example of a disagreement
paragraphs: Therapist A says: "I think we should prepare the rooms immediately after each session."
Therapist B says: "I think it would be better to prepare them shortly before the next appointment."
Both employees have different opinions. They can discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each approach and follow the agreed workplace procedure.

sections.title: Example of conflict
paragraphs: Therapist A says: "Your suggestion is ridiculous. You don't know what you're talking about."
Therapist B responds: "You're always trying to control everybody!"
The disagreement has now become personal.

sections.title: 4. Why understanding the causes of conflict matters
1. It helps employees identify problems early
paragraphs: Recognising warning signs allows employees to address issues before they escalate.

sections.title: 2. It improves communication
paragraphs: Employees learn to ask questions and clarify information rather than making assumptions.

sections.title: 3. It strengthens teamwork
paragraphs: Colleagues can cooperate more effectively when they understand and respect one another's responsibilities.

sections.title: 4. It protects workplace relationships
paragraphs: Early intervention can prevent minor frustrations from becoming lasting resentment.

sections.title: 5. It supports a respectful work environment
paragraphs: Employees become better equipped to manage differences without hostility.

sections.title: 6. It protects client service
paragraphs: A cooperative team is better able to maintain smooth appointments, room preparation and client care.

sections.title: 5. Cause 1: Poor communication
paragraphs: Poor communication is one of the most common causes of workplace conflict.
It occurs when information is unclear, incomplete, delayed, inaccurate or misunderstood.
Clear communication reduces unnecessary misunderstandings.

sections.title: Example — an uncommunicated appointment change
paragraphs: A receptionist changes a client's appointment from 2 p.m. to 3 p.m. but forgets to inform the assigned therapist.
The therapist prepares for the original appointment time. Later, she becomes upset because the schedule was changed without her knowledge. The receptionist responds defensively. An argument begins.
The main issue was not necessarily that either employee disliked the other. The problem was a communication failure.

sections.title: How to prevent poor communication
list: Communicate important changes promptly.
Confirm that instructions have been understood.
Ask questions when information is unclear.
Use appropriate communication channels.
Avoid assuming that another employee already knows.
Keep relevant records accurate.

sections.title: 6. Cause 2: Unclear responsibilities
paragraphs: Conflict can arise when employees do not understand who is responsible for a particular task.
Sometimes responsibilities are clear, but an employee fails to complete them. In such situations, the problem is not unclear instructions. It is failure to follow through.
Employees should distinguish between these situations before assigning blame.

sections.title: Example — shared room supplies
paragraphs: Two therapists share responsibility for preparing a treatment room. Each assumes the other will replenish the supplies. Neither completes the task.
When the next appointment approaches, both begin blaming each other.
The responsibility was not clearly assigned or confirmed.

sections.title: How to prevent unclear responsibilities
list: Understand your assigned responsibilities.
Clarify shared duties.
Confirm handover arrangements.
Ask a supervisor when responsibilities are unclear.
Avoid assuming that a colleague will complete a task without agreement.

sections.title: 7. Cause 3: Different personalities and working styles
paragraphs: Employees have different personalities, habits, communication preferences and approaches to work.
Some employees are naturally quiet. Others are expressive. Some prefer detailed instructions. Others prefer brief explanations. Some work quickly, while others are more methodical.
These differences do not automatically create conflict. However, conflict may arise when employees interpret differences as personal problems.
Employees do not need identical personalities to work successfully together.

sections.title: Example — a brief appointment update
paragraphs: A receptionist speaks directly and briefly when communicating appointment updates. A therapist interprets her communication as rude. The receptionist believes she is simply being efficient.
Neither employee understands the other's perspective.

sections.title: How to prevent personality-based conflict
list: Avoid assuming negative intentions.
Communicate expectations clearly.
Respect different working styles.
Ask questions when tone or meaning is unclear.
Focus on professional behaviour rather than personality preferences.

sections.title: 8. Cause 4: Gossip, rumours and misinformation
paragraphs: Gossip occurs when employees discuss other people's private matters, mistakes or behaviour unnecessarily, particularly when the information is unverified or not appropriate to share.
Rumours can create suspicion and distrust.
A rumour can create a conflict even when the original allegation is false.

sections.title: Example — speculation about a supervisor
paragraphs: An employee tells another colleague: "I heard the supervisor doesn't like you. That's why she keeps correcting your work."
The colleague becomes upset and begins interpreting every correction as personal hostility. Later, it becomes clear that the statement was based on speculation.

sections.title: Consequences of gossip and rumours
list: Damaged trust.
Misunderstandings.
Unnecessary suspicion.
Workplace divisions.
Retaliation.
Distraction from responsibilities.

sections.title: How to prevent gossip and rumours
list: Avoid spreading unverified information.
Do not discuss confidential matters unnecessarily.
Ask for clarification from the appropriate person.
Refuse to participate in conversations intended to ridicule colleagues.
Report serious concerns through proper channels.

sections.title: 9. Cause 5: Perceived unfairness and favouritism
paragraphs: Employees may become resentful when they believe responsibilities, opportunities or corrections are distributed unfairly.
Employees may not always know the full circumstances of another person's situation.
Different outcomes do not automatically prove favouritism. However, genuine inconsistency can damage trust.
Fairness is important both in practice and in how decisions are communicated.

sections.title: Example — two late arrivals
paragraphs: Two employees arrive late on separate occasions. One receives a formal correction. The other appears to receive no response.
The first employee begins to believe that management favours the second.

sections.title: How employees can prevent this conflict
list: Avoid drawing conclusions from incomplete information.
Raise concerns respectfully.
Focus on specific examples.
Follow established reporting channels.

sections.title: How supervisors can prevent this conflict
list: Apply standards consistently.
Explain expectations clearly.
Avoid personal favouritism.
Consider relevant circumstances fairly.
Protect confidential employee information.

sections.title: 10. Cause 6: Poor attitude and disrespectful behaviour
paragraphs: Workplace conflict can arise when employees speak or behave disrespectfully.
Respectful communication can prevent a simple misunderstanding from becoming a personal disagreement.
list: Insults.
Mockery.
Sarcasm intended to humiliate.
Shouting.
Dismissive responses.
Unnecessary interruptions.
Public embarrassment.
Refusal to communicate respectfully.

sections.title: Example — a booking clarification
paragraphs: A therapist asks a receptionist for clarification about a booking. The receptionist replies: "Can't you read? Must I explain everything to you?"
The therapist becomes offended. The original question was simple, but the response creates tension.
Better response: "The booking was moved to 4 p.m. Let me show you the updated schedule."

sections.title: 11. Cause 7: Failure to complete responsibilities
paragraphs: When one employee repeatedly fails to perform assigned duties, other employees may be forced to compensate. Over time, frustration can develop.
Teamwork does not mean that responsible employees must continually cover for avoidable neglect without the issue being addressed.
Helping colleagues is valuable, but accountability remains important.

sections.title: Example — repeated unfinished rooms
paragraphs: A therapist repeatedly leaves treatment rooms unprepared. Other therapists must complete the unfinished tasks before attending to their clients.
They begin feeling that the workload is unfair. Eventually, a disagreement occurs.

sections.title: How to prevent conflict from unfinished work
list: Complete assigned duties reliably.
Communicate early when unable to complete a task.
Avoid leaving unfinished work without an appropriate handover.
Acknowledge genuine mistakes.
Report repeated operational problems through appropriate channels.

sections.title: 12. Cause 8: Stress, fatigue and workload pressure
paragraphs: Busy periods can increase tension.
Employees may become tired, impatient or frustrated when managing multiple responsibilities.
Stress may explain why someone reacts poorly, but it does not justify disrespectful behaviour.

sections.title: Example — a busy reception
paragraphs: Several clients arrive close together. The receptionist is managing calls and appointment confirmations. Therapists are preparing rooms and attending to clients.
An employee asks for assistance. Another responds sharply because she feels overwhelmed. A disagreement begins.
The immediate trigger was the sharp response. However, workload pressure may have contributed.

sections.title: How to prevent conflict during busy periods
list: Communicate workload difficulties early.
Request assistance when necessary.
Prioritise urgent responsibilities.
Avoid taking frustration out on colleagues.
Support one another during busy periods.
Inform supervisors when workload arrangements are becoming difficult to manage.

sections.title: 13. Cause 9: Competition, jealousy and comparison
paragraphs: Unhealthy competition can create conflict when employees become more concerned about outperforming colleagues than supporting the team.
A colleague's success does not reduce your value.

sections.title: Example — client praise
paragraphs: A therapist receives positive feedback from several clients. Another therapist becomes jealous and begins making negative remarks about her work. The relationship becomes strained.

sections.title: Warning signs
list: Resenting colleagues' achievements.
Deliberately withholding useful information.
Making negative comparisons.
Trying to undermine another employee.
Treating recognition as a personal threat.

sections.title: How to prevent unhealthy competition
list: Celebrate genuine achievements.
Focus on personal improvement.
Share knowledge appropriately.
Avoid comparing employees unnecessarily.
Recognise that individual excellence contributes to team success.

sections.title: 14. Cause 10: Unresolved past disagreements
paragraphs: Some workplace conflicts continue because earlier disagreements were never properly addressed.
Resolving a conflict does not require employees to become close personal friends.
It requires them to maintain appropriate professional cooperation and respect.

sections.title: Example — an old handover argument
paragraphs: Two employees argued several weeks ago about a shift handover. They never discussed the matter afterward.
Now, whenever one raises a concern, the other assumes she is acting out of resentment. Even ordinary conversations become tense.

sections.title: How to prevent unresolved conflict from continuing
list: Address concerns promptly.
Avoid storing up resentment.
Discuss unresolved issues respectfully.
Apologise when appropriate.
Seek supervisory assistance when direct discussion is unsuccessful.
Avoid bringing unrelated past disputes into every new disagreement.

sections.title: 15. Cause 11: Assumptions and misunderstandings
paragraphs: Conflict frequently begins when employees assume they know another person's intentions.
Some concerns may be genuine, but employees should avoid treating assumptions as established facts.
Before reacting to what you think happened, try to understand what actually happened.

sections.title: Example — an unanswered greeting
paragraphs: A receptionist walks past a therapist without greeting her. The therapist assumes: "She's deliberately ignoring me because she doesn't like me." She becomes cold toward the receptionist.
However, the receptionist was distracted by an urgent client issue and did not notice her. The conflict developed from an assumption.
Instead of immediately assuming hostility, the therapist can observe the situation and seek clarification if necessary.

sections.title: Common harmful assumptions
list: "She corrected me because she hates me."
"They didn't invite me because they don't respect me."
"She didn't reply because she's deliberately ignoring me."
"Management assigned that task because they want to punish me."

sections.title: 16. Cause 12: Poor leadership and inconsistent instructions
paragraphs: Workplace conflict does not always begin with employees.
Supervisory decisions and communication can also create unnecessary tension.
Employees should seek clarification when instructions conflict rather than guessing which direction to follow.

sections.title: Example — conflicting supervisor instructions
paragraphs: A supervisor tells one therapist to prepare a room immediately. Another supervisor later gives a conflicting instruction.
The therapist becomes confused. When the task is not completed as expected, she is blamed.

sections.title: How leadership can prevent conflict
list: Provide clear instructions.
Coordinate changes in responsibilities.
Avoid contradictory directions.
Communicate expectations consistently.
Listen to employee concerns.
Correct misunderstandings promptly.
Acknowledge management errors when they occur.

sections.title: 17. How small problems become major conflicts
paragraphs: Many conflicts develop gradually.
The earlier a problem is addressed constructively, the easier it may be to prevent escalation.
Employees should not wait until resentment becomes hostility before raising legitimate concerns.
list: An issue occurs. A task is missed or information is misunderstood.
An assumption is made. An employee believes the mistake was deliberate.
Emotions intensify. Frustration, embarrassment or resentment develops.
Communication becomes hostile. Accusations, insults or defensive responses begin.
The conflict spreads. Other employees take sides or cooperation breaks down.

sections.title: 18. The ROOT method for identifying the cause of conflict

items.label: R — Recognise the issue
items.body: Identify what happened without immediately assigning blame.

items.label: O — Observe the facts
items.body: Separate what is known from assumptions, rumours and emotional interpretations.

items.label: O — Open respectful communication
items.body: Ask questions, listen and allow relevant perspectives to be explained.

items.label: T — Take an appropriate step
items.body: Clarify responsibilities, correct the problem or involve a supervisor when necessary.

sections.title: ROOT example
paragraphs: Two therapists argue because a treatment room was not ready.
Instead of immediately deciding who is at fault, the supervisor applies ROOT.
The supervisor identifies the missed preparation, reviews the handover arrangement, listens to both employees and clarifies who is responsible for replenishing supplies after each session.
The immediate issue is resolved, and the handover process becomes clearer.
Understanding the cause of conflict is often more useful than simply deciding who argued first.

sections.title: Case study A: The missed appointment update
paragraphs: A receptionist changes an appointment but fails to inform the assigned therapist. The therapist becomes upset and accuses the receptionist of deliberately making her work difficult.
Expected lesson: Communication failures and negative assumptions can combine to create unnecessary conflict.
list: What was the original cause of the disagreement?
What assumption did the therapist make?
How did the accusation affect the situation?
What should the receptionist acknowledge?
What communication process could prevent recurrence?

sections.title: Case study B: The unfinished room preparation
paragraphs: A therapist repeatedly leaves shared supplies unreplenished. Other therapists become frustrated. One colleague eventually insults her in front of everyone.
Expected lesson: Failure to complete responsibilities can create legitimate concerns, but disrespectful responses make resolution harder.
list: What operational problem caused the frustration?
Was the frustration understandable?
Did the insult help resolve the issue?
What responsibility belongs to the therapist?
When should a supervisor become involved?

sections.title: Case study C: The rumour
paragraphs: An employee hears that management intends to remove her from a particular responsibility. Without confirming the information, she accuses a colleague of influencing the decision. The colleague denies the allegation, and the two stop cooperating.
Expected lesson: Unverified information can damage workplace relationships.
list: What role did the rumour play?
What facts were missing?
Why was the accusation inappropriate?
How should the employee seek clarification?
How can the relationship be repaired?

sections.title: Case study D: The busy reception
paragraphs: Several clients arrive close together. The receptionist is handling calls and appointment confirmations. A therapist requests information, but the receptionist responds rudely. The therapist reacts angrily.
Expected lesson: Workload pressure can contribute to conflict, but respectful communication and practical support remain necessary.
list: What pressure contributed to the situation?
What behaviour escalated the disagreement?
How could the receptionist communicate more appropriately?
What could the therapist do differently?
What operational support might reduce similar incidents?

sections.title: 20. Practical group activity: Identify the real cause
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees recognise the causes of workplace conflict before deciding how to respond.
Divide participants into small groups. The trainer should present each situation. Participants should identify the likely cause of conflict and suggest one preventive action.
Expected outcome: Participants should understand that identifying the root cause is essential to preventing repeated conflict.

items.label: 1. Two employees assume the other person will replenish shared supplies.
items.body: Cause: Unclear responsibilities. Prevention: Confirm who completes the handover and ask a supervisor if it is still unclear.

items.label: 2. A receptionist changes an appointment but does not inform the therapist.
items.body: Cause: Poor communication. Prevention: Pass on schedule changes promptly and confirm they have been received.

items.label: 3. An employee tells colleagues that management dislikes another staff member without evidence.
items.body: Cause: Gossip, rumours and misinformation. Prevention: Do not spread unverified claims. Seek clarification through the appropriate channel if a genuine concern exists.

items.label: 4. An employee becomes hostile because a colleague received public praise.
items.body: Cause: Competition, jealousy and comparison. Prevention: Treat a colleague's recognition as team success, not a personal threat.

items.label: 5. Two colleagues remain resentful after an earlier disagreement was never addressed.
items.body: Cause: Unresolved past disagreements. Prevention: Discuss the original issue respectfully or involve a supervisor if direct discussion is unsuccessful.

items.label: 6. An employee interprets a colleague's brief reply as deliberate disrespect.
items.body: Cause: Assumptions and misunderstandings. Prevention: Ask what was meant instead of treating the assumption as a fact.

sections.title: Group reflection
paragraphs: Each group should discuss one realistic workplace disagreement and identify:
list: The original issue.
Any assumptions or emotional reactions.
The main cause of the conflict.
One action that could have prevented escalation.

sections.title: 21. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 1 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is workplace conflict? Any situation where employees have different personalities / A disagreement, tension or dispute that affects workplace relationships or cooperation / Every correction given by a supervisor
Two employees each assume the other will complete a shared task. What is the likely cause of conflict? Unclear responsibilities / Jealousy / Personal attack
Which behaviour is most likely to escalate a workplace disagreement? Asking for clarification / Discussing the issue privately / Making personal accusations and involving colleagues in taking sides

What should an employee do after hearing an unverified rumour about a colleague? Share it with the entire team / Avoid spreading it and seek appropriate clarification if necessary / Immediately confront the colleague with an accusation

What does the ROOT method encourage? Recognising the issue, observing facts, opening respectful communication and taking appropriate action / Reacting immediately, opposing colleagues and transferring blame / Remaining silent about every disagreement

sections.title: 22. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what workplace conflict means.
Describe the difference between disagreement and conflict.
Identify ten common causes of workplace conflict.
Explain how poor communication can create conflict between receptionists and therapists.
Describe how unclear responsibilities can lead to blame-shifting.
Explain how gossip and rumours can damage workplace relationships.
Describe how workload pressure may contribute to conflict without excusing disrespectful behaviour.
Explain the difference between genuine unfair treatment and perceived unfairness.
Describe how assumptions can turn an ordinary situation into a disagreement.
Explain the ROOT method in your own words.
Identify three workplace habits you intend to develop to prevent unnecessary conflict.
Describe one realistic workplace disagreement and explain how it could have been prevented.

sections.title: 23. Seven-day conflict-awareness challenge
table: Notice common situations that create tension during work
Clarify responsibilities instead of making assumptions
Avoid gossip and unverified workplace rumours
Apply the ROOT method to a minor workplace concern
Reflect on how your behaviour can help prevent unnecessary conflict

sections.title: 24. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Workplace conflict can arise from many causes, including poor communication, unclear responsibilities, personality differences, gossip, unfair treatment, disrespectful behaviour, workload pressure and unresolved disagreements.
Not every conflict begins because someone deliberately intends to cause trouble.
Sometimes a misunderstanding, incomplete instruction or missed responsibility creates tension.
However, employees can make matters worse through accusations, insults, assumptions, retaliation or involving others unnecessarily.
At Zura Spa, employees should learn to recognise the original cause of a disagreement, communicate respectfully, clarify facts and address problems before they escalate.
Supervisors should also maintain clear expectations, fair treatment and appropriate communication.
Next topic: Understanding Disagreement Versus Disrespect.

remember: Many workplace conflicts begin with small issues that could have been resolved through honesty, communication and mutual respect. Do not allow assumptions, frustration or personal pride to turn a simple problem into a lasting disagreement. At Zura Spa, we build a stronger team by understanding the real causes of conflict, taking responsibility for our actions and choosing cooperation over unnecessary hostility. The goal is not to prove who is superior, but to create a workplace where everyone can perform their responsibilities effectively and respectfully.
